name: Fort Dearborn — store house

documented_range.note: THE RANGE IS THE FORT'S, NOT THIS BUILDING'S. No source reached dates any individual building inside Fort Dearborn. It opens with the rebuild of 1816 and closes with the demolition of the fort's principal structures in the summer of 1856 (Andreas). What carries the scene date is the middle: the post was garrisoned continuously from June 1832 to 29 December 1836.

placement.position_note: READ OFF THE 1830 HARRISON PLAN. Position in pixels on the plate Andreas reproduces at vol. 1 p. 113, scaled at 1.10 ft per pixel (the derivation is on fort_dearborn_palisade and in docs/RESEARCH/fort_dearborn.md section 3), rotated to the sheet's true-north arrow, and hung on the fort centre at local E +1152, N +221. Carry +/-20 percent on the offset from the fort centre and +/-20 m on the fort itself. Hubbard, 1827: 'The store-house and guard-house were on either side of the southern gate'. This record takes the eastern of the two buildings the 1830 plan draws there; the argument for that assignment is on fort_dearborn_guard_house and it rests on where Hubbard's next clause puts the magazine.
placement.symbolic_location: Inside the south wall of Fort Dearborn, immediately east of the south gate, fronting north onto the parade.

footprint.note: NO SOURCE GIVES THIS BUILDING'S SIZE. 12.24 x 4.37 m (about 40 x 14 ft) is the eastern of the two small south-wall buildings as drawn on the 1830 plan at the derived scale. Same warning as its neighbour: the depth is a fourteen-pixel measurement.

kind.note: Hubbard names a store-house beside the southern gate in 1827; Andreas's summary of the rebuilt fort lists a 'provision-store' among what the stockade enclosed. GUARD: Robert Fergus's 1850 account puts a storehouse on the EAST side of the parade with the barracks and the artillery house. That is the compound of the 1850s, twenty years after the pickets came down, and where the 1830 plan and an 1827 eyewitness agree with each other this project follows them.

construction.note: Not stated. Log by the same argument as the barracks.

stories.note: Not attested; single storey is the type for a provision store of this footprint and it is how the 1830 plan draws it.

wall_height_m.note: No height attested. About nine feet: one storey with the head-room a stacked provision store wants.

roof_type.note: Not attested; gable is the type.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested for any building in this fort. 34 degrees is the archetype's mid-range for a shingled or riven-shake roof of this period and span, inferred from construction practice rather than measured.

chimneys.note: A COUNT OF ZERO IS A CLAIM, NOT AN ABSENCE. A provision store is the one building in a fort you do not want a fire in, and nothing describes a stack on this one. The record says none and the model builds none.

function.note:
The garrison's provision store. Destroyed with the barracks in the September 1827 lightning fire and standing again on the 1830 plan; see fort_dearborn_barracks for what that does and does not establish.

THE ARMY'S OWN CONTRACT NOTICES NAME THIS BUILDING AND SAY WHAT WENT IN AT ITS DOOR (T-1591). Two printings of the Fort Dearborn beef proposals — Chicago Democrat 28 May 1834, claim chicago_democrat_1834_05_28#c006, and 4 June 1834, claim chicago_democrat_1834_06_04#c013 — require the contractor's fresh beef to be delivered in quarters 'at the store house of Fort Dearborn', which the second printing calls 'the subsistance store house of Fort Dearborn', 'in such quarters and at such times as the Assistant Commissary of Subsistence may require', not more than three times a week nor less than once, 'amounting probably to 400 pounds per week'. So this range was the post's PROVISION store: the receiving door for the garrison's meat, worked by the commissary, reached by a contractor's cart two or three mornings a week. The weekly poundage is the notice's own estimate of what the garrison ate and is recorded as an estimate. WHAT IS NOT TAKEN FROM IT: the notices do not say which range, which face or which door, so no position, footprint or opening is changed here — the fort's buildings stand where the 1830 survey and Andreas put them. Nor is the thirteen-month gap to the scene date closed: the fresh-beef contract advertised over the same fort in the scene month names no building at all.

land_owner.value: The ground was entered by John Baptist Baubian, 28 May 1835
land_owner.note: THE UNITED STATES RESERVATION. This is the same tract L108 already derives for `1835_no_build_ground.json` — from G1, Madison's line and the traced waterline — so the polygon is inherited rather than built again, and `check.sh` already re-derives it. The register's own row is the second, independent witness to the date L108 quotes from Andreas: Beaubien's pre-emption, 28 May 1835, five weeks before the scene date. The derived polygon is short of the documented 75.69 acres for the reasons L108 states, and is a floor rather than the reservation. WHETHER THE ENTRY HELD IS NOT READ HERE: it was disputed, and this row records the entry the register carries and nothing about its outcome. THE MARGIN IS 62 m: this footprint stands that far inside the tract's nearest boundary, which is more than twice the working horizontal uncertainty of anything traced off the 1834 sheets (about 20 m), so the assignment survives the error the construction carries. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

what_it_supplies: that a named trade was being carried on in Chicago in a named week, and often where
self-reported addresses, which are the strongest address evidence this project has: the advertiser was paying, and his customers had to find him
dissolution, removal and replacement notices — the only thing that keeps a documented business out of the 1835 town under the owner's ruling 3
post-office letter lists, naming residents by the hundred (ruling 1: a listed name mints a resident candidate, flagged letter_list_only)
the village and later town ordinances, printed complete — the 7 November 1833 code is the richest single item in the run
arrivals and clearances, which date the piers and the harbour as working structures
public notices that fix a building as a polling place, an auction site or a meeting place on a given day
the paper's own imprint, self-reported: the corner of South Water and Clark streets
twenty-one months of continuous weekly attestation ending three weeks before the scene date, including the issue printed on 1835-07-01
what_it_does_not_supply: any building's form, material, storey count, fenestration or dimensions — an advertisement describes a trade, not a building
the specific corner of any junction it names: 'on the corner of' does not say which of the four
anything at all from an engraving — see trap 1; the cuts are the printer's stock
proof that a business named in 1833 or 1834 still stood on 1835-07-01; that is ruling 3's survival liberty, and it is a liberty
an argument from silence, unless corpus.json shows the issues either side of the silence are both in the deposit
a reading that outranks a scan read of the same passage — see ruling 2 and the C. & I. HARMON case
a citation without an issue page and column

what_it_supplies: the fort's plan arrangement: a quadrangular picket enclosure, corner works, four ranges, two gates
which building stood on which side of the parade
the relative proportions of the enclosure and the buildings in it
the fort's rotation relative to true north
the named ground around the fort: garrison garden, cultivated field, barn, wash house, well, shop, cemetery, ferry
what_it_does_not_supply: any dimension in feet - there is no scale bar
elevations, heights, roof forms or materials
the state of the fort in 1835 - it is five years earlier
a separation between the 1830 survey and the settler-memory additions the plate admits to

research_note: The eastern building at the south gate. Nothing distinguishes it from its neighbour in the sources except its name and the side it stands on, and this project's reason for putting it east rather than west is written on fort_dearborn_guard_house.
